subject: math
title: Grade 8 Probability of Two Independent Events
seo_title: Grade 8 Probability of Two Independent Events Worksheets: Free Math with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Theoretical probability with two independent events
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 math worksheets on the probability of two independent events for the BC curriculum: sample spaces with tables and tree diagrams, multiplying probabilities as fractions, decimals and percents, probability trees, and predictions compared with results. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: For two independent events, multiply: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
key_sub: A coin and a number cube give 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes, so P(heads and 6) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12, not 1/2 + 1/6. Expected count = probability × number of trials.
body_html:
Independent events and sample spaces

Two events are independent when one does not change the chance of the other. A coin cannot change how a spinner lands. Taking a marble and NOT putting it back changes the jar, so those picks are not independent.

The sample space is the list of all outcomes. Show it with a tree diagram or a table. Count the outcomes by multiplying: a 3-section spinner and a coin give 3 × 2 = 6 outcomes.

Example 1

You spin both spinners in the table. What is P(even number and blue)?

2B and 4B are 2 of the 12 equally likely outcomes.

Answer: 212 = 16

Multiply the probabilities

For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). This works even when the outcomes are not equally likely. On a probability tree, multiply along each path. If more than one path works, add those paths.

Example 2

You roll a number cube and toss a coin. What is P(5 or 6, and heads)?

P(5 or 6) = 26 and P(heads) = 12. 26 × 12 = 212.

Answer: 212 = 16

Example 3

What is the probability that Ryan makes exactly one of two free throws?

Make, miss: 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24. Miss, make: 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.24. Add the two paths.

Answer: 0.48

Making predictions

Expected number = probability × number of trials. Real results are usually close to the prediction, but rarely exactly the same. More trials usually get closer.

Example 4

You toss a coin and roll a number cube 120 times. About how many times would you expect heads and a 6?

P(heads and 6) = 112. 112 of 120 = 120 ÷ 12 = 10.

Answer: about 10

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
P(heads and 6) = 12 + 16 = 46“And” for independent events: multiply. 12 × 16 = 112.
A 4-section and a 3-section spinner give 4 + 3 = 7 outcomes.Multiply: 4 × 3 = 12 outcomes.
12 and 15 give 27.Multiply the tops and the bottoms: 110.
0.3 × 0.3 = 0.9Count the decimal places: 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09.
Product of 4 on two 1–4 spinners: only 1 × 4 and 2 × 2.4 × 1 is a different outcome: 3 cells.
“Doubles came up 3 times, so they are less likely now.”Cubes have no memory. It is still 16.

faq.q: What are independent events in Grade 8 math?
faq.a: Two events are independent when the result of one does not change the chance of the other, like tossing a coin and rolling a number cube. Taking two marbles from a bag without putting the first one back is not independent.

faq.q: How do you find the probability of two independent events?
faq.a: Multiply the two probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). For heads and a 6, 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. You can check by counting the outcomes in a table or tree diagram.

faq.q: Why do you multiply probabilities instead of adding them?
faq.a: Both events must happen, so the chance is smaller than either one alone. Adding gives a bigger number, like 1/2 + 1/6 = 4/6, and can even go over 1.

faq.q: How do you use probability to make a prediction?
faq.a: Multiply the probability by the number of trials. With a 1/12 chance and 120 turns, expect about 10 results; real results are usually close but rarely exact.

sets.title: Sample spaces: tables and tree diagrams

items.q: A spinner has 3 equal sections, A, B and C. You spin it and toss a coin. How many outcomes does the tree diagram show?
items.e: Each of the 3 spinner branches splits into 2 coin branches: 3 × 2 = 6 outcomes. 5 comes from adding 3 + 2.

items.q: Which outcome is NOT in the sample space?
items.e: The spinner only has A, B and C, so DH can’t happen. The other three are at the end of a branch.

items.q: How many outcomes show tails?
items.e: AT, BT and CT: 3 outcomes. Every spinner branch has one tails branch.

items.q: You spin a number spinner (1 to 4) and a colour spinner (red, blue, green). How many outcomes are in the table?
items.e: 4 rows × 3 columns = 12 outcomes. 7 comes from adding 4 + 3.

items.q: How many outcomes show an even number and green?
items.e: Even numbers are 2 and 4, so 2G and 4G: 2 outcomes. 4 counts every green outcome.

items.q: How many outcomes show red?
items.e: The red column has 1R, 2R, 3R and 4R: 4 outcomes. 12 is the whole table.

items.q: How many outcomes show a number greater than 2 and NOT blue?
items.e: Numbers 3 and 4 with red or green: 3R, 3G, 4R, 4G, so 4 outcomes. 6 counts every outcome with 3 or 4. 8 counts every outcome that is not blue.

items.q: You roll a number cube and spin a spinner with 4 equal sections. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: Each of the 6 numbers goes with each of the 4 sections: 6 × 4 = 24. 10 comes from adding 6 + 4.

items.q: A spinner has 5 equal sections. You spin it twice. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: Each of the 5 results on the first spin goes with each of the 5 on the second: 5 × 5 = 25. 10 comes from adding 5 + 5.

items.q: You spin two spinners, each with 4 equal sections numbered 1 to 4, and multiply the numbers. How many outcomes give a product of 4?
items.e: 1 × 4, 2 × 2 and 4 × 1: 3 outcomes. 2 forgets that 1 × 4 and 4 × 1 are different outcomes.

items.q: How many outcomes give an odd product?
items.e: The product is odd only when both numbers are odd: 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes (1, 3, 3, 9). 12 is the number of even products.

items.q: Which product appears in the most cells?
items.e: 4 is in 3 cells (1 × 4, 2 × 2, 4 × 1). Every other product is in 1 or 2 cells, so 4 is the most likely product. 16 is the largest product, but it is in only one cell.

items.q: Kai picks a hoodie (grey or navy) and a cap (black, white or red). In a tree diagram, how many branches end on the right side?
items.e: Each of the 2 hoodies splits into 3 caps: 2 × 3 = 6 end branches, one for each outfit. 5 adds 2 + 3.

items.q: You toss a nickel and a dime. Which list shows the sample space?
items.e: Each coin can land H or T: 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes, HH, HT, TH, TT. HT (nickel heads) and TH (dime heads) are different outcomes.

items.q: Which pair of events is independent?
c: Drawing two cards from a deck without putting the first back
Picking a team captain, then a co-captain from the other players
Taking two granola bars from a box without putting the first back
Rolling a number cube and tossing a coin
items.e: A coin cannot change how a number cube lands, so a number cube and a coin are independent. In the other pairs, the first pick changes what is left for the second.

items.q: Which pair of events is NOT independent?
c: Tossing a coin and spinning a spinner
Picking two names from a hat without putting the first back
items.e: When the first name stays out, there are fewer names left, so the chance for the second pick changes. Those events are not independent. Coins, cubes and spinners have no memory.

items.q: Ava says, “A spinner with 4 sections and a spinner with 3 sections give 4 + 3 = 7 outcomes.” What is wrong?
c: Each of the 4 results pairs with all 3: 4 × 3 = 12
There are only 4 outcomes, from the bigger spinner
items.e: Result 1 can go with each of the 3 sections, and so can 2, 3 and 4. That is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 4 × 3 = 12 outcomes. Multiply, don’t add.

items.q: You take a marble, put it back, and take a marble again. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: The marble goes back, so the second pick also has 4 colours: 4 × 4 = 16. 8 adds 4 + 4. 12 = 4 × 3 would be right only if the first marble stayed out.

items.q: You make an outcome table for a coin and a spinner with 8 equal sections. How many cells with outcomes does it have?
items.e: 2 rows × 8 columns = 16 cells. 10 adds 2 + 8. 64 is 8 × 8, as if there were two spinners.

items.q: Two independent events have 18 outcomes in all. The first event is a coin toss. How many outcomes does the second event have?
items.e: 2 × ? = 18, so the second event has 18 ÷ 2 = 9 outcomes. 16 subtracts 18 − 2.

items.q: What is the probability of 3 and red?
items.e: 3R is 1 of the 12 equally likely outcomes: 112. 712 adds 14 + 13. 17 adds 4 + 3 outcomes.

items.q: What is the probability of an even number and blue?
items.e: 2B and 4B: 2 of 12 outcomes, so 212 (= 16). 24 only looks at the number spinner.

items.q: What is the probability of a number less than 4 and NOT green?
items.e: 1, 2 or 3 with red or blue: 3 × 2 = 6 of 12 outcomes, so 612 (= 12). 812 counts every outcome that is not green, even with a 4.

items.q: What is the probability that the product is 6?
items.e: 2 × 3 and 3 × 2: 2 of 16 cells, so 216 (= 18). 29 treats the 9 different products as equally likely. 616 uses the product as the count.

items.q: What is the probability that the product is even?
items.e: Only odd × odd is odd (4 cells), so 16 − 4 = 12 cells are even: 1216 (= 34). 816 guesses that half are even. 69 counts the different products, not the cells.

items.q: What is the probability that the product is greater than 8?
items.e: 9, 12, 12 and 16: 4 of 16 cells, so 416 (= 14). 316 counts 12 only once, but 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 are different outcomes.

items.q: You roll two number cubes. What is the probability that the sum is 8?
items.e: 2 + 6, 3 + 5, 4 + 4, 5 + 3, 6 + 2: 5 of 36 cells, so 536. 336 counts each pair in one order only. 111 treats the 11 sums as equally likely.

items.q: What is the probability that the sum is less than 5?
items.e: Sum 2: 1 cell, sum 3: 2 cells, sum 4: 3 cells. 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, so 636 (= 16). 1036 also counts the sum of 5, which is not less than 5.

items.q: You roll two number cubes. What is the probability that both numbers are greater than 4?
items.e: Each cube has 2 numbers greater than 4 (5 and 6): 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes (5-5, 5-6, 6-5, 6-6), so 436 (= 19). 236 counts only 5-5 and 6-6. 23 adds 13 + 13.

items.q: What is the probability of A and heads?
items.e: AH is 1 of the 6 outcomes: 16. 56 adds 13 + 12. 13 forgets the coin.

items.q: What is the probability of NOT A and tails?
items.e: BT and CT: 2 of 6 outcomes, so 26 (= 13). 46 counts every outcome that is not A, with heads too.

items.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, blue, yellow and green. You spin it twice. What is the probability of two different colours?
items.e: Same colour happens in 4 of the 4 × 4 = 16 outcomes, so different colours happen in 12: 1216 (= 34). 616 counts red-blue but not blue-red.

items.q: You toss a coin and roll a number cube. What is the probability of heads OR a 6 (or both)?
items.e: H1 to H6 is 6 outcomes, plus T6: 7 of 12, so 712. 812 counts H6 twice. 112 is heads AND 6.

items.q: What is the probability of 4 and green, as a percent?
items.e: 4G is 1 of 12 outcomes: 112 = 1 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.083, so about 8%. About 58% is 712, from adding 14 + 13. 12% just writes the 12 as a percent.

items.q: What is the probability that the sum is 7 or 11?
items.e: Sum 7 is in 6 cells and sum 11 is in 2 cells (5 + 6, 6 + 5): 6 + 2 = 8, so 836 (= 29). 436 counts each pair in one order only.

items.q: You roll a red number cube and a blue number cube. What is the probability that the red number is greater than the blue number?
items.e: 36 outcomes, 6 of them are doubles. The other 30 split evenly: red greater in 15, blue greater in 15. So 1536. 1836 forgets the doubles. 2136 includes the doubles. 636 is the chance of doubles.

items.q: A jar has 4 marbles: red, blue, green and yellow. You take one, put it back and take another. What is the probability of red both times?
items.e: Red, red is 1 of the 4 × 4 = 16 outcomes: 116. 24 adds 14 + 14. 112 forgets that the marble goes back.

items.q: With the same jar (one marble of each colour, put back each time), what is the probability of the same colour both times?
items.e: Red-red, blue-blue, green-green, yellow-yellow: 4 of 16, so 416 (= 14). 116 counts only one colour. 1216 is the chance of different colours.

items.q: What is the probability of NOT getting 1 and red?
items.e: 1R is 1 of the 12 outcomes, so the other 1112 are not. 34 is the chance of not spinning 1. 23 is the chance of not red.

items.q: Which is more likely: a sum of 6 with two number cubes, or a product of 4 with two spinners numbered 1 to 4?
c: A product of 4 with the spinners
A sum of 6 with the number cubes
items.e: Sum of 6: 5 of 36 ≈ 0.14. Product of 4: 3 of 16 ≈ 0.19. 0.19 > 0.14, so a product of 4 with the spinners is more likely.

items.q: A and B are independent. P(A) = 12 and P(B) = 15. What is P(A and B)?
items.e: Multiply: 12 × 15 = 110. 710 adds. 27 adds the tops and the bottoms. 17 adds the bottoms.

items.q: A and B are independent. P(A) = 23 and P(B) = 34. What is P(A and B)?
items.e: 23 × 34 = 612 = 12. 1712 adds and is more than 1. 89 cross-multiplies as if dividing.

items.q: You spin this spinner and toss a coin. What is P(yellow and tails)?
items.e: P(yellow) = 23 (2 of 3 equal sections). 23 × 12 = 26 (= 13). 14 treats yellow and green as equally likely. 76 adds.

items.q: A and B are independent. P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.7. What is P(A and B)?
items.e: 5 × 7 = 35, with two decimal places: 0.5 × 0.7 = 0.35. 1.2 adds and is more than 1. 0.035 and 3.5 put the decimal point in the wrong place.

items.q: A and B are independent. P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.3. What is P(A and B)?
items.e: 3 × 3 = 9, with two decimal places: 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09. 0.9 has only one decimal place. 0.6 adds.

items.q: A and B are independent. P(A) = 40% and P(B) = 25%. What is P(A and B)?
items.e: Change to decimals: 0.4 × 0.25 = 0.1 = 10%. 65% adds. 1000% multiplies 40 × 25 without changing to decimals.

items.q: Ryan makes a free throw with probability 0.6. His shots are independent. What is P(make, make)?
items.e: Multiply along the path: 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36. 1.2 adds. 0.6 is one shot only.

items.q: What is P(miss, miss)?
What is the probability that Ryan makes exactly one of the two shots?
items.e: Two paths work. Make, miss: 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24. Miss, make: 0.4 × 0.6 = 0.24. Add the paths: 0.48. 0.24 uses only one path. 1 adds 0.6 + 0.4.

items.q: A spinner lands on green with probability 14 and on white with probability 34. You spin it twice. What is P(white, white)?
items.e: 34 × 34 = 916. 64 adds and is more than 1. 68 adds the tops and the bottoms. 116 is green, green.

items.q: What is the probability of at least one green?
items.e: Every outcome except white, white has a green: 1 − 916 = 716. 24 adds 14 + 14. 616 is exactly one green and forgets green, green.

items.q: You take a marble, put it back, and take another. What is P(blue, blue)?
items.e: The marble goes back, so P(blue) = 25 both times. 25 × 25 = 425. 220 forgets to put the marble back (25 × 14). 45 adds.

items.q: Same jar, the marble is put back. What is P(red, then blue)?
items.e: 35 × 25 = 625. Adding 35 + 25 = 1 would mean it is certain. 620 forgets to put the marble back.

items.q: You roll a number cube and spin a spinner with 4 equal sections, one of them blue. What is P(even number and blue)?
items.e: P(even) = 36 = 12 and P(blue) = 14. 12 × 14 = 18. 34 adds. 26 adds the tops and the bottoms.

items.q: A and B are independent. P(A) = 12 and P(A and B) = 110. What is P(B)?
items.e: P(A) × P(B) = P(A and B), so P(B) = 110 ÷ 12 = 15. Check: 12 × 15 = 110. 120 multiplies instead of dividing. 25 subtracts.

items.q: Two independent events each have a probability between 0 and 1. What is true about P(A and B)?
c: It is always 12
It is greater than both P(A) and P(B)
It is less than both P(A) and P(B)
items.e: Multiplying by a number less than 1 makes a number smaller. Both events happening is less likely than either one alone. If your answer is bigger, you probably added.

items.q: A spinner has 5 equal sections numbered 1 to 5. You spin it and toss a coin. What is P(prime number and heads), as a decimal?
items.e: 2, 3 and 5 are prime, so P(prime) = 35 = 0.6. 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3. 1.1 adds. 0.6 forgets the coin.

items.q: You roll two number cubes. What is P(6 on the first cube and an odd number on the second)?
items.e: 16 × 36 = 336 = 112. 46 adds. 16 forgets the second cube.

items.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections numbered 1 to 10. You spin it twice. What is the probability of 10 both times, as a percent?
items.e: 110 × 110 = 1100 = 1%. 20% adds 10% + 10%. 10% is one spin only.

items.q: Zara says, “P(heads and 5) is 12 + 16 = 46.” What is wrong?
c: She should multiply: 12 × 16 = 112
Nothing, 46 is right
She should subtract: 12 − 16 = 26
She should add the bottoms: 18
items.e: Both events must happen, so multiply: 112. H5 is 1 of the 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes. Adding gives a bigger chance, but “both” should be less likely than one alone.

items.q: You toss two coins 80 times. About how many times would you expect two heads?
items.e: P(HH) = 14. 14 of 80 = 80 ÷ 4 = about 20. About 27 uses 13, as if HT and TH were one outcome. About 60 is NOT two heads.

items.q: You toss a coin and roll a number cube 120 times. About how many times would you expect heads and a 6?
items.e: P(heads and 6) = 112. 120 ÷ 12 = about 10. About 80 uses 46 (adding). About 15 uses 18 (adding 2 + 6 outcomes). About 20 forgets the coin.

items.q: You spin both spinners 160 times. About how many times would you expect a product of 4?
items.e: P(product 4) = 316. 160 ÷ 16 = 10, and 10 × 3 = about 30. About 10 counts only one cell. About 18 uses 19, treating the 9 products as equally likely.

items.q: Ji-woo tossed two coins 60 times. What is the experimental probability of HH?
items.e: HH came up 18 times in 60: 1860 = 0.3. 0.25 is the theoretical probability. 0.18 uses the count as the decimal. 0.7 is NOT HH.

items.q: How many times does the theory predict HH in 60 tosses?
items.e: 14 of 60 = 15. 18 is what actually happened. 20 uses 13, as if there were only 3 outcomes.

items.q: Which statement about Ji-woo’s results is true?
c: They are close to the theory, as expected
HH should have come up exactly 15 times
TT is now due to come up more often
items.e: Results almost never match the theory exactly. 18 HH and 15 TT are close to the 15 predicted, so the results are close to the theory. Coins have no memory, so nothing is “due”.

items.q: Four students toss two coins. Whose experimental probability of HH is most likely to be closest to 14?
items.e: More trials usually give an experimental probability closer to the theory, so 1000 tosses.

items.q: Mei rolls two number cubes and gets doubles 3 times in a row. What is the probability of doubles on her next roll?
items.e: The cubes have no memory. Doubles is 6 of 36 outcomes on every roll: 16. 1216 is the chance of 3 doubles in a row, worked out before any rolls.

items.q: Game A: you win on heads and a 6 (coin and number cube). Game B: you win if two spinners numbered 1 to 4 both land on 4. Which game gives a better chance to win?
items.e: Game A: 12 × 16 = 112. Game B: 14 × 14 = 116. 112 > 116, so Game A.

items.q: Hana wins if the product is even. Kai wins if it is odd. Is the game fair?
c: No, Kai wins 1216 of the time
Yes, even and odd are equally likely
No, Hana wins 1216 of the time
items.e: 12 of the 16 cells are even and only 4 are odd. Hana is 3 times as likely to win, so the game is not fair.

items.q: Arjun wins if the sum of two number cubes is even. Nadia wins if it is odd. Is the game fair?
c: No, Arjun wins more: doubles are always even
No, Nadia wins more: odd sums include 7
No, Arjun wins more: 6 of the 11 sums are even
Yes, each has 18 of the 36 outcomes
items.e: Count cells, not sums. 18 cells are even and 18 are odd, so the game is fair. The 11 sums are not equally likely.

items.q: You spin this spinner and toss a coin 200 times. About how many times would you expect red and heads?
items.e: P(red and heads) = 34 × 12 = 38. 38 of 200 = about 75. About 50 treats red and blue as equally likely. About 100 forgets the spinner, and about 150 forgets the coin.

items.q: Two groups toss two coins. Group 1: 8 HH in 20 tosses (0.4). Group 2: 52 HH in 200 tosses (0.26). Which result is the better estimate of P(HH)?
c: Group 1, because it used fewer tosses
Group 2, because it has more trials
items.e: More trials give a more reliable estimate. 0.26 is also close to the theory, 14 = 0.25. So Group 2.

items.q: Simran spins two spinners 50 times. The outcome 3 and red came up 6 times. The theoretical probability is 112. Using the theory, about how many times would you predict 3 and red in 600 spins?
items.e: 112 of 600 = 600 ÷ 12 = about 50. About 72 uses her experimental result 650, which is based on only 50 spins. About 100 uses 16.

items.q: You want to expect about 5 results of heads and a 6 (coin and number cube). About how many turns do you need?
items.e: Heads and 6 happens 112 of the time. 5 × 12 = about 60 turns. About 40 uses 18 (adding 2 + 6 outcomes). About 30 forgets the coin.

items.q: Owen predicts a sum of 7 about 33 times in 360 rolls of two number cubes, because there are 11 sums. Leah predicts about 60 times. Who is right?
c: Both, the numbers are close enough
Owen: each sum is 111
items.e: The 11 sums are not equally likely. A sum of 7 is in 6 of the 36 cells, so 636 × 360 = 60. Leah is right.

items.q: In 100 rolls of two number cubes, both numbers were even 31 times. What is the theoretical probability that both are even, as a percent?
items.e: 12 × 12 = 14 = 25%. 31% is the experimental result. 50% is one cube only. 9% comes from the 9 even-even cells, but there are 36 cells, not 100.

items.q: Sofia tosses two coins. P(HH) was 0.27 after 100 tosses and 0.252 after 1000 tosses. What do you expect after 10 000 tosses?
c: About 0.234, because it keeps going down
items.e: With more trials the experimental probability gets close to 0.25, the theoretical value. It is rarely exactly 0.25, and it does not keep moving in one direction.

items.q: Ryan makes a free throw with probability 0.6, and his shots are independent. He goes to the line for 2 shots 50 times. About how many times would you expect him to make both shots?
items.e: P(make, make) = 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36. 0.36 × 50 = about 18. About 30 uses 0.6 for one shot. About 60 adds 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2, which is more than every trip.

items.q: Which prediction is greater: two heads in 100 tosses of two coins, or doubles in 120 rolls of two number cubes?
items.e: Two heads: 14 × 100 = 25. Doubles: 636 × 120 = 20. 25 > 20, so two heads, about 25.

sets.title: Word problems: games, sports and trips

items.q: On a BC Ferries sailing from Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay, Liam picks a meal at random from 4 meals (one is fish and chips) and a drink at random from 3 (one is apple juice). What is the probability of fish and chips with apple juice?
items.e: 4 × 3 = 12 meal-and-drink outcomes, so 112. 712 adds 14 + 13. 14 forgets the drink.

items.q: A Grade 8 class in Vancouver draws its field trip at random: Stanley Park, Grouse Mountain or Science World, on one of the 5 school days. What is the probability of Grouse Mountain on a Friday?
items.e: 3 places × 5 days = 15 outcomes: 115. 815 adds 13 + 15. 18 adds 3 + 5 outcomes.

items.q: Nadia takes a bus and then the SkyTrain to school. The bus is on time with probability 0.9 and the SkyTrain with probability 0.8. Assume the two are independent. What is the probability that both are on time?
items.e: 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72. 1.7 adds and is more than 1. 0.072 has one decimal place too many. 0.98 is the chance that at least one is on time.

items.q: In hockey, Noah scores on a shootout attempt with probability 0.3. His attempts are independent. What is the probability that he misses two attempts in a row?
items.e: P(miss) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7. 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49. 1.4 adds. 0.21 is score, then miss. 0.09 is scoring both.

items.q: At Whistler, Ji-woo picks one of 4 chairlifts at random, then one of 6 runs from the top at random. What is the probability that she picks one certain chairlift and one certain run?
items.e: 4 × 6 = 24 outcomes: 124. 110 adds 4 + 6 outcomes. 1024 adds 14 + 16.

items.q: In a board game, Chloe needs a sum of 9 or more on two number cubes. What is the probability?
items.e: Sum 9: 4 ways, 10: 3, 11: 2, 12: 1. 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 of 36, so 1036 (= 518). 411 treats the sums as equally likely. 636 counts each pair in one order only. 436 is a sum of 9 only.

items.q: Mateo’s bike lock has 2 dials, each with the digits 0 to 9. He forgot the code and tries one combination at random. What is the probability that it opens, as a percent?
items.e: 10 × 10 = 100 combinations, so 1100 = 1%. 5% uses 10 + 10 = 20 outcomes. 20% adds 10% + 10%.

items.q: Sofia’s fun fair game: a player wins on heads and a number greater than 4 on a number cube. She expects 180 players. About how many prizes should she bring?
items.e: P(win) = 12 × 26 = 16. 180 ÷ 6 = about 30. About 150 adds 12 + 13. About 90 forgets the cube, and about 60 forgets the coin.

items.q: A Burnaby class of 25 draws one name each day for 2 days to pick the class helper. The name goes back in after each draw. What is the probability that Zara is picked both days?
items.e: 125 × 125 = 1625. 225 adds. 150 uses 25 + 25 outcomes. 1600 forgets that the name goes back in.

items.q: Same draw: what is the probability that Zara is picked on at least one of the 2 days?
items.e: Not picked both days: 2425 × 2425 = 576625. At least once: 1 − 576625 = 49625. 225 (= 50625) counts picked-both-days twice. 48625 is exactly one day.

items.q: Owen guesses two multiple-choice questions, each with 4 choices. What is the probability that he gets both right, as a percent?
items.e: 14 × 14 = 116 = 0.0625 = 6.25%. 50% adds 25% + 25%. 12.5% uses 4 + 4 = 8 outcomes. 25% is one question.

items.q: Same two guesses: what is the probability that Owen gets both wrong?
items.e: P(wrong) = 34 for each. 34 × 34 = 916. 64 adds. 316 is right, then wrong.

items.q: A whale-watching tour from Victoria sees orcas on a trip with probability 0.8. Assume trips are independent. Leah goes on 2 trips. What is the probability she sees orcas on both?
items.e: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64. 1.6 adds. 0.16 is orcas on the first trip but not the second.

items.q: On a hike in the Okanagan, Zara picks one of 3 trails at random and one of 4 snacks at random. What is the probability that she does NOT pick the lake trail but does pick granola?
items.e: P(not lake trail) = 23 and P(granola) = 14. 23 × 14 = 212 (= 16). 112 is the lake trail with granola.

items.q: Kai wants a fun fair game with a 110 chance of winning. Which game works?
c: Heads on a coin and 5 on a spinner numbered 1 to 5
Heads on a coin and 6 on a number cube
items.e: 12 × 15 = 110. The others are 112, 14 and 13.

items.q: Kai expects 250 players at his game with a 110 chance of winning. About how many prizes should he bring?
items.e: 110 of 250 = about 25. About 175 adds 12 + 15. About 125 uses the coin only, and about 50 uses the spinner only.

items.q: Nadia’s soccer team picks a jersey colour at random (red, white or blue) and a sock colour at random (red, white or blue). What is the probability that the jersey and socks match?
items.e: 3 × 3 = 9 outcomes, and 3 of them match: 39 (= 13). 19 counts one colour only. 36 adds 3 + 3 outcomes.

items.q: Two lacrosse teams in Coquitlam each pick a captain at random. Team A has 15 players (Lucas is one). Team B has 12 players (Emma is one). What is the probability that Lucas and Emma are both picked?
items.e: 115 × 112 = 1180. 320 adds. 127 adds 15 + 12 players. 227 adds the tops and the bottoms.

items.q: A game uses a coin and a spinner with equal sections, one of them green. P(heads and green) = 112. How many sections does the spinner have?
items.e: 12 × 16 = 112, so 6 sections (2 × 6 = 12 outcomes). 12 forgets the coin. 10 subtracts 12 − 2.

items.q: Ryan can play Game A (win on two heads with two coins) or Game B (win on tails and a 5 or 6 on a number cube). Which game should give more wins in 60 turns, and about how many?
items.e: Game A: 14 × 60 = 15. Game B: 12 × 26 = 16, and 16 × 60 = 10. So Game A, about 15. About 20 forgets the coin in Game B.
